tier_reason: The repository holds only README.md and src/apex_memmove.{c,cpp,h}. The README says 'fastest memcpy/memmove on x86/x64 ... EVER (according to the author)'. No benchmark code, numbers or baseline appear anywhere in it, and the source comments only compare the author's own variants (memmove09, memmove40/41, mm04). The CodeProject article, the PostgreSQL thread and the Ultimate++ forum post do not resolve from this environment (ENOTFOUND), so no numbers could be checked.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 14 stars, 1 fork; code by Trevor Herselman (2014), mirrored by rukkal in 2016. Discussed on Hacker News as 'Apex memmove', on the PostgreSQL mailing list in July 2016 (Alvaro Herrera raised licence compatibility and asked for real-workload gains; snippet only) and in a 2020 Ultimate++ forum thread (snippet only).
corrections.caveats: Tier D: a self-description with no numbers in the repository. A search-result snippet of a 2020 Ultimate++ forum post reports one user's single MSVC run on a Core i7: apex_memcpy averaged 3.55 ms against 4.37 ms for the CRT memcpy, with clang similar. Neither the block size nor the flags appear in the snippet. The page could not be opened, so none of it is claimed here. The same snippet notes that the code has no licensing information. The CodeProject article is the only methodology source, and codeproject.com does not resolve from here. A CodeProject message titled 'Bug' exists on the article (codeproject.com/Messages/5374685/Bug), but its content could not be read. The mirror has three commits, all dated 2016-09-22, and no tests or benchmark code, so the claim cannot be reproduced from the repository. The dispatcher points apex_memcpy and apex_memmove at the same routine, so memcpy pays the overlap handling. It selects a variant by CPUID: SSE4.2 is taken as a proxy for fast unaligned access (kryptonite), SSSE3 selects tiberium and SSE2 alone selects mithril (32-bit only); every other target falls back to the C library. The code targets 2014-era CPUs, long before ERMS and FSRM made rep movsb competitive in glibc and the MSVC CRT. The .c and .cpp files are near-identical copies.

notes: Kept at tier D with no number on any reachable page. The main shortcomings are no benchmark and no license, so it is reference only, and the repository is an abandoned 2016 mirror with 14 stars. Low notability is a tag here, not a reject, under the keep-and-document rule. The only known number (3.55 ms vs 4.37 ms, one MSVC run on a Core i7) is snippet only; if the Ultimate++ forum or the CodeProject article opens elsewhere, it could support tier C. No license text was found anywhere, and is_fork_of and the license were left uncorrected.
